title: Averages and measures of spread
summary: An [[average|average]] is one typical value: the [[mean|mean]], the [[median|median]] or the [[mode|mode]]. The [[range-of-a-data-set|range]] is a [[measure-of-spread|measure of spread]]: it shows how spread out the values are. You'll find each from a list or a table, and pick the right average for the job.

goals.text: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a list of values.
Find the mean, median and mode from a [[frequency-table|frequency table]].
Choose the best average for a purpose, with a reason.
Find the [[quartile|quartiles]] and the [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]], and say what they show.
Work out an [[estimate|estimate]] of the mean from a [[grouped-frequency-table|grouped frequency table]].
Write down the [[modal-class|modal class]] of grouped data.

before.hint: Count three figures from the first non-zero digit, then look at the next digit.
before.explain: The first three figures are $4$, $7$ and $3$. The next digit is $8$, so round up: $47.4$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.9}}.

before.prompt: A table shows the scores $1$, $2$ and $3$ with frequencies $7$, $12$ and $5$. How many scores are there altogether?
before.hint: Each frequency counts how many times that score happened.
before.explain: Add the frequencies, not the scores: $7 + 12 + 5 = 24$. Revise it in {{lesson:9.1}}.

blocks.text: What is a typical number of books read in a month? There are three useful answers.

blocks.statement: The [[mean|mean]] is the total of the values divided by the number of values.

blocks.question: Eight students read these numbers of books last month: $3, 0, 4, 1, 3, 6, 2, 3$. Calculate the mean.
steps: Add all the values. Include the $0$, because it is a value: $3 + 0 + 4 + 1 + 3 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 22$.
Count the values: there are $8$.
Divide the total by the count: $22 \div 8 = 2.75$.
The mean need not be one of the values.

blocks.statement: The [[median|median]] is the middle value when the values are in order. For $n$ values, it is the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value.
blocks.plain: Line the values up and take the one in the middle.

blocks.text: With an even number of values there are two middle values. The median is halfway between them: add them and divide by $2$.

blocks.question: The heights of six seedlings, in cm, are $7.4, 5.9, 8.1, 6.6, 9.0, 6.2$. Find the median.
steps: Put the values in order: $5.9, 6.2, 6.6, 7.4, 8.1, 9.0$.
There are $6$ values, so the median is the $\frac{6+1}{2} = 3.5$th value. That is halfway between the 3rd and 4th values.
The 3rd and 4th values are $6.6$ and $7.4$.
Halfway between them: $\frac{6.6 + 7.4}{2} = \frac{14}{2} = 7$.

blocks.hint: Put the values in order first.
blocks.explain: In order: $7, 13, 26, 32, 43$. There are $5$ values, so the median is the $\frac{5+1}{2} = 3$rd value, $26$. $43$ is the middle of the unordered list, and $3$ is only the position.

blocks.statement: The [[mode|mode]] is the value that occurs most often.

blocks.text: A data set can have more than one mode if values tie for most often. If every value occurs only once, there is no mode.
If you know the mean, you can find the total: total $=$ mean $\times$ number of values. Then you can find a missing value.

blocks.prompt: The mean of six numbers is $7$. Five of the numbers are $5, 13, 6, 8$ and $2$. Find the sixth number.
blocks.hint: The total of all six is $6 \times 7$.
blocks.explain: The total of all six is $6 \times 7 = 42$. The five you know add to $34$, so the sixth is $42 - 34 = 8$.

blocks.text: To combine two groups of different sizes, don't average their means. Find each group's total, add the totals, then divide by the total number of values.
Two classes can have the same mean but very different marks. An average doesn't show how spread out the values are.

blocks.statement: The [[range-of-a-data-set|range]] is the largest value minus the smallest value.
blocks.plain: How far the values stretch, from bottom to top.

blocks.text: The range is a [[measure-of-spread|measure of spread]]. A small range means the values are close together. It is always one number, not a pair of values.

blocks.question: The midday temperatures in a town for one week, in $^{\circ}\text{C}$, are $3, -2, 5, -6, 1, 4, 0$. Find the range.
steps: The largest value is $5$. The smallest is $-6$, the coldest day.
Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest $= 5 - (-6)$.
Subtracting a negative is adding: $5 + 6 = 11$.

blocks.question: Aisha's long jumps, in metres, are $4.12, 4.35, 3.98, 4.27, 4.40$. Ben's are $4.05, 4.61, 3.72, 4.48, 4.19$. Find the range of each, in metres. Who is more consistent?
steps: Aisha: largest $4.40$, smallest $3.98$. Range $= 4.40 - 3.98 = 0.42$ m.
Ben: largest $4.61$, smallest $3.72$. Range $= 4.61 - 3.72 = 0.89$ m.
Aisha's range is smaller, so her jumps are closer together. She is more consistent.

blocks.prompt: Find the mean of the same temperatures: $3, -2, 5, -6, 1, 4, 0$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Keep the minus signs when you add.

blocks.prompt: Six numbers have a range of $25$. Five of them are $31, 44, 27, 38$ and $40$. Find the two possible values of the sixth number.
blocks.hint: These five have a range of only $17$.
blocks.explain: It is a new largest, $27 + 25 = 52$, or a new smallest, $44 - 25 = 19$.

blocks.text: A [[frequency-table|frequency table]] is a short way to write a long list. A value with frequency $9$ appears $9$ times in the list.
For the total of the values, multiply each value $x$ by its frequency $f$, then add. This is $\sum fx$, where $\sum$ means "add them all up".
The bottom line, $\sum f$, is the total frequency: how many values there are. It is not the number of rows.

blocks.question: A survey asks families how many pets they have. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Pets} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 8 & 13 & 9 & 7 & 3 \end{array}$ Calculate the mean number of pets.
steps: Multiply each number of pets by its frequency: $0 \times 8 = 0$, $1 \times 13 = 13$, $2 \times 9 = 18$, $3 \times 7 = 21$, $4 \times 3 = 12$.
Add these to get the total number of pets: $\sum fx = 0 + 13 + 18 + 21 + 12 = 64$.
Add the frequencies to get the number of families: $\sum f = 8 + 13 + 9 + 7 + 3 = 40$.
Divide: $64 \div 40 = 1.6$.

blocks.text: On Paper 3 or 4 your calculator can find the mean from the table. Still write down the division, such as $64 \div 40$.

blocks.question: A football team records the goals it scores in each match. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{Goals} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 4 & 7 & 6 & 5 & 2 & 1 \end{array}$ Find the median number of goals.
steps: Total frequency: $4 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 25$ matches. The median is the $\frac{25+1}{2} = 13$th value.
Keep a running total: $4$, then $4 + 7 = 11$, then $11 + 6 = 17$.
So values 12 to 17 are all $2$ goals, and the 13th value is $2$.

blocks.prompt: For the same football table, write down the mode.
blocks.hint: The mode is a number of goals, not a frequency.
blocks.explain: The highest frequency, $7$, is in the row for $1$ goal, so the mode is $1$. The $7$ counts matches, not goals.

blocks.prompt: Scores $2$, $3$ and $4$ have frequencies $5$, $8$ and $7$. Work out the mean score.
blocks.hint: Find $\sum fx$, then divide by the total frequency.
blocks.explain: $\sum fx = 10 + 24 + 28 = 62$ and $\sum f = 20$, so the mean is $62 \div 20 = 3.1$. Dividing by the $3$ rows gives $20.7$.

blocks.text: 1. The mean uses every value. But one very large or very small value, an extreme value, pulls it away from the rest.
2. The median is the middle value, so an extreme value hardly moves it. Use it when the data have an extreme value.
3. The mode is the most common value. Use it for the most popular choice, or when the data are words, such as colours.
The range uses only the two end values, so one extreme value changes it a lot.

blocks.question: Seven people's journey times to school, in minutes, are $26, 32, 29, 27, 31, 88, 30$. Find the median. Explain why it describes a typical journey better than the mean.
steps: In order: $26, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 88$. The median is the 4th value, $30$.
The mean is $263 \div 7 = 37.57\ldots$, longer than six of the seven journeys.
The extreme value $88$ pulls the mean up, but not the median.

blocks.question: A shoe shop sells these sizes on Saturday: $6, 8, 7, 8, 5, 9, 8, 7, 6, 8, 10, 7$. The manager will order more of the size that sells best. Which average should she use? Find it.
steps: The mean is $89 \div 12 = 7.41\ldots$. Nobody bought that size.
In order: $5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10$. The median is halfway between the 6th and 7th values, $7.5$. Nobody bought a $7.5$ either.
The mode is the size sold most often. Size $8$ sold $4$ times, more than any other.
So she should use the mode.

blocks.prompt: Eight friends have between $150$ and $400$ followers online. A ninth has $25\,000$. Which average best shows a typical number?
blocks.explain: The $25\,000$ is an extreme value. It drags the mean far above everyone else, but not the median.

blocks.prompt: Which average can you find for the favourite colours of a class?
blocks.hint: Can you add colours, or put them in order of size?
blocks.explain: You can't add colours or put them in order of size. You can only count which is most common.

blocks.text: The range depends on the two most extreme values. A better measure of spread looks only at the middle half of the data.

blocks.statement: Order the values and split them into two halves. The lower [[quartile|quartile]] is the middle of the lower half; the upper quartile is the middle of the upper half.
blocks.plain: With the median, the quartiles cut the data into four equal parts.

blocks.text: With an odd number of values, leave the median out of both halves. With an even number, just cut the ordered list in half.

blocks.statement: The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] (IQR) is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.
blocks.plain: The spread of the middle half of the data.

blocks.text: The IQR ignores the bottom and top quarters, so one extreme value hardly changes it.

blocks.question: Eleven runners' times, in seconds, are $12.4, 13.1, 11.8, 14.6, 12.9, 13.5, 12.2, 15.3, 13.0, 12.7, 14.1$. Find the interquartile range.
steps: The median is the 6th value, $13.0$. Leave it out: each half has $5$ values.
Lower half: $11.8, 12.2, 12.4, 12.7, 12.9$. Its middle value is the lower quartile, $12.4$.
Upper half: $13.1, 13.5, 14.1, 14.6, 15.3$. Its middle value is the upper quartile, $14.1$.

blocks.alt: The eleven runners' times in order in a row of boxes. The 3rd box, 12.4, is the lower quartile. The 6th box, 13.0, is the median. The 9th box, 14.1, is the upper quartile. A bracket from the lower to the upper quartile is labelled IQR equals 1.7. The five boxes before the median are labelled lower half and the five after it upper half.
blocks.caption: The quartiles are the middles of the two halves.

blocks.text: Finding the quartiles from the list as it was given. Put the values in order first, just as for the median.

blocks.question: Ten phone batteries last these numbers of hours: $8.4, 9.1, 7.6, 10.3, 8.9, 9.7, 7.9, 10.8, 9.4, 8.2$. Find the interquartile range.
steps: Ten is even, so there is no median value to leave out. Cut the list in half.
Lower half: $7.6, 7.9, 8.2, 8.4, 8.9$, so the lower quartile is $8.2$.
Upper half: $9.1, 9.4, 9.7, 10.3, 10.8$, so the upper quartile is $9.7$.

blocks.prompt: Nine students' marks in a test are $67, 72, 58, 81, 64, 75, 69, 88, 61$. Find the interquartile range.
blocks.hint: After ordering, leave out the median. Each half has $4$ values, so its middle is halfway between two values.
blocks.explain: In order: $58, 61, 64, 67, 69, 72, 75, 81, 88$. The lower quartile is $\frac{61 + 64}{2} = 62.5$ and the upper quartile is $\frac{75 + 81}{2} = 78$. IQR $= 78 - 62.5 = 15.5$.

blocks.prompt: Data has one extreme value. Why is the IQR a better measure of spread than the range?
blocks.hint: Which values does each measure use?

options.text: The extreme value hardly affects it

blocks.explain: The IQR uses only the middle half of the data. The range uses the extreme value itself.

verify.truth: The extreme value hardly affects it

blocks.text: A [[grouped-frequency-table|grouped frequency table]] puts the values into groups. Each group is a [[class-interval|class interval]], such as $150 < h \le 160$: more than $150$, up to and including $160$.
You don't know the exact values. So treat every value in a class as its [[midpoint|midpoint]], halfway between the boundaries: $\frac{150 + 160}{2} = 155$. The mean is then an estimate.

blocks.question: The table shows the heights of a group of students. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Height } h\text{ (cm)} & 140 < h \le 150 & 150 < h \le 160 & 160 < h \le 170 & 170 < h \le 180 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 7 & 23 & 26 & 9 \end{array}$ Calculate an estimate of the mean height. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: Multiply each midpoint by its frequency: $145 \times 7 = 1015$, $155 \times 23 = 3565$, $165 \times 26 = 4290$, $175 \times 9 = 1575$.
Divide: $10\,445 \div 65 = 160.69\ldots \approx 161$ cm.

blocks.text: Multiplying by the upper boundary or the class width instead of the midpoint. Each class is represented by the value halfway between its boundaries.
Discrete data can be grouped too, such as $20$–$29$ goals. Find the midpoint from the smallest and largest value in the class.

blocks.question: The table shows the number of passengers on a ferry's crossings in one month. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Passengers} & 57\text{–}63 & 64\text{–}70 & 71\text{–}77 & 78\text{–}84 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 32 & 53 & 37 & 29 \end{array}$ Calculate an estimate of the mean number of passengers. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: Divide: $10\,558 \div 151 = 69.92\ldots \approx 69.9$.

blocks.prompt: Quiz marks are grouped as $51$–$59$, $60$–$68$ and $69$–$77$, with frequencies $5$, $12$ and $8$. Estimate the mean, correct to three significant figures.
blocks.explain: Midpoints $55$, $64$ and $73$. $\sum f \times \text{midpoint} = 275 + 768 + 584 = 1627$ and $\sum f = 25$, so the estimate is $1627 \div 25 = 65.08 \approx 65.1$.

blocks.prompt: Write down the midpoint of the class $35 < m \le 42$.
blocks.hint: Add the two boundaries and halve.

blocks.statement: When the classes all have the same width, the [[modal-class|modal class]] is the class with the highest frequency.

blocks.prompt: The table shows the distances some people walk each day. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Distance } d\text{ (km)} & 0 < d \le 2 & 2 < d \le 4 & 4 < d \le 6 & 6 < d \le 8 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 8 & 15 & 21 & 6 \end{array}$ Write down the modal class.
blocks.hint: Answer with a class, not a frequency.
blocks.explain: The highest frequency is $21$, so the modal class is $4 < d \le 6$. The $21$ is a frequency, not a class.

blocks.text: Median: put the values in order and take the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th (halfway between the middle two when $n$ is even). Mode: the most common value. Range: largest $-$ smallest.

blocks.tex: \text{mean from a frequency table} = \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}

blocks.text: An extreme value pulls the mean, not the median. Use the mode for the most popular choice.
Quartiles: the medians of the lower and upper halves (leave out the median when $n$ is odd). IQR $=$ upper quartile $-$ lower quartile.
Modal class: the class with the highest frequency, when the classes have equal widths.

mistakes: Dividing by the number of rows in a frequency table. Divide $\sum fx$ by the total frequency $\sum f$.
Giving the position $\frac{n+1}{2}$ as the median. The median is the value in that position.
Dropping minus signs when you add or subtract negative values.
Giving one answer when a missing value has to make the range bigger. It can be a new largest or a new smallest.
examTips: Calculate the mean: write the division, such as $64 \div 40$, before the answer. That line earns the method mark.
Leave an exact answer such as $1.6$ as it is. Round to 3 s.f. only when the decimal goes on.
Give a reason why the mean is not suitable: name the extreme value and say it pulls the mean away from most of the data.
